prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B030 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange, my reasons are firmer than in round 1 because the arguments for it now come from several directions that do not depend on one another. The physics is a single idea with a decisive realization. Trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength cancels the lattice light shift on the clock transition and suppresses Doppler and recoil effects, so that a large ensemble can be interrogated with ion-like accuracy. Katori proposed this and demonstrated it early; Ye's group drove the systematic evaluation, the many-body interaction shifts and the comparison technology to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18. From my own field the key point is that the ensemble statistics, the collisional and interaction shifts in a degenerate or dense lattice gas, and the control of them are physics in the strict sense, not only engineering; that answers the discovery-versus-invention question Danielsson raised. Independent laboratories in several countries agree at this level, which is the maturity evidence a measurement achievement can offer, and no member has argued for delay. The two-name credit is the one place where the shortlist does not force an arbitrary cut. I record that the case rests on demonstrated performance alone and not on the pending redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of individual trapped quantum systems) remains the most serious reservation, and I still do not regard it as dismissed by assertion. After round 1 I can state the distinction I would defend: those prizes honoured a ruler and single-ion control, while the lattice clock is a different scheme, resting on the magic-wavelength condition, that obtains the statistics of many neutral atoms without the trap perturbing the transition. That sentence is sufficient for me and the overlap is no longer disqualifying, but the citation must carry it. The two-name allocation is a judgement and not a clean fact, as Pearce says: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups made real contributions to accuracy and the committee will be criticised for omitting them. Last, a prize ahead of the redefinition leaves the largest practical payoff prospective.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize covered, would not name Lemonde in the citation, and would not rest the case on the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: In round 1 I said the overlap could not be treated as closed. Her argument and Kroll's, together, answer the chair's question for me: the new element is the magic-wavelength condition and the many-atom neutral system built on it, which neither earlier prize contained, and that is what the citation should name. I therefore move from holding the overlap as an open worry to treating it as answered, provided the citation says lattice clocks and not optical timekeeping in general. I also agree with her on Lemonde: naming him would not repair the allocation and would blur the invention-plus-realization basis. I accept the omission as a cost and not as an error.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B020 to B030 but keeps the concern that a lattice-clock prize is a third award in one metrology lineage and an instrument achievement whose discovery content must be argued through fundamental-physics tests.
responses.response: I think his own list of consequences carries the argument: redshift tests at millimetre scale, searches for varying constants and ultralight dark matter, and relativistic geodesy exist because a quantum system now has a known frequency to eighteen digits, and that required new physics on light shifts, forbidden transitions, blackbody shifts and interactions in the lattice gas. That is the kind of result I would call physics. I would not rest the citation on those applications, though, since several are still prospective; the citation should rest on the invention and what has been measured. I agree with him that the overlap must be answered in the text, and I think the one-sentence distinction does that.

responses.point: Kroll argues that Boulder's systematic evaluation to 10^-18 and into the many-body regime is as much part of the history as Katori's proposal, and that Ye's accuracy record could be read as a series of performance refinements.
responses.response: The last caution is the right one and I take it seriously. My reading is that Ye's contribution is more than successive records: the control of many-body interaction shifts and the comparison technology changed what can be done with the concept, and that is why dropping either name would misstate the history. I share his view, and Eriksson's and Olsson's, that the redefinition of the second should not delay the award. On B004, which he and I both hold as an alternative, I repeat that I would not defend Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger against Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, so I do not see B004 as a competitor this year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 alone, says our shared stake in simulation methods means our agreement should count for little, and argues that the method turned density functional theory into a tool for thermodynamics, diffusion and melting.
responses.response: His caveat about our shared bias is fair and I keep B022 only as a fallback because of it. I do not doubt the attribution or the maturity, and his answer on the 2013 chemistry prize is reasonable. My difficulty is that the entry is a method, with its main uses in materials science and chemistry, and the committee has not settled whether a computational method counts as a physics invention; only the two of us ranked it. I note that he would not stand in the way of B030 on the merits and would defer on the technical priority questions, so I read his position as a competing preference and not as an objection, and I would not change my configuration to it.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, stresses that the two-name allocation is a judgement and not a clean fact, and that the case should rest on demonstrated performance rather than on the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree and I would put it on the record in that form: the allocation to Katori and Ye is the committee's judgement that the conceptual origin and the decisive demonstration of ultimate performance are identifiable, and other groups contributed. On B020, I still hold it as a genuine discovery and I would return to it if three defensible names were agreed, but Pearce himself called the AMANDA and IceCube credit a larger attribution problem than anything in B030, so I cannot support it as the preferred part. If B030 were set aside, my single alternative would be B004 with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, with B022 behind it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, and metrology experts outside it, will accept the one-sentence distinction between the lattice clock and the 2005 comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes; I can state it but I cannot test it against the community.

Whether the Katori and Ye allocation survives expert scrutiny of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups; I cannot settle this from the supplied text, and the detailed priority record is recalled and not independently verified by me.
I cannot confirm from the supplied material whether the redefinition of the second has taken place; I do not make the case depend on it, but it affects how much practical impact is already realised.
If B030 stalls, the choice among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller for B004 remains contested within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B030, B004 or B022: none of Katori, Ye, Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger, Car or Parrinello appears among my documented co-authors or supervisors, and my research fields (turbulent transport, statistical physics, neural networks) are not those of the credited names. I note Eriksson's point that I share an interest in simulation methods with the B022 case, and I treat my second alternative with that in mind.
